#7647. Breaking news: a new James Bond has been chosen!

The new James Bond has been announced!! Finally, after five years of waiting (since Daniel Craig departed the franchise with/in 2021’s sentimental No Time to Die), we have a new 007.

There has been much, much speculation about who would be the new Bond—the eighth actor to play Bond (in a legitimate adaptation… go away, 1967’s Casino Royale), and the star of the twenty-sixth Bond film. Would it be Slow Horses‘s Jack Lowden? Perhaps Josh O’Connor or Callum Turner? What about a dark horse, like CrimeReads favorite Josh Bowman? Remember way back when, when we all thought it would be Idris Elba? And remember how after that, we all thought it would be Aaron Taylor-Johnson?

Nope! Turns out, the next James Bond will be….

Yes, Robert Pattinson, the creative and hardworking English actor who will likely be nominated for a Supporting Actor Academy Award for his role as Antinous in Christopher Nolan’s The Odyssey, this year. Robert Pattinson! Robert Pattinson is Bond!

The Bond franchise has the power to catapult an actor from a lesser-known realm into wild international fame. As I wrote previously,

The individuals I refer to as the James Bond Selection Committee chose Daniel Craig last time; a well-respected actor of stage and screen, known mostly for supporting roles. The point of Bond casting is not to choose someone so closely associated with another leading man role that it becomes distracting; the actor must fully embody Bond.

This time, the selection committee chose Mr. Franchise, himself! Cedric Diggory of Harry Potter, Edward Cullen of Twilight (no matter how hard he tries to forget it), and Batman of The Batman! He’s about to be in Dune: Part III.

Pattinson, who is 40, has worked with countless extraordinary filmmakers in many challenging parts, distancing himself from the heartthrobby roles he played in his youth. He has already lead films directed by David Cronenberg, Claire Denis, Bong Joon Ho, Werner Herzog, the Safdie Brothers, Robert Eggers, James Gray, Lynne Ramsay, Christopher Nolan, Fernando Meirelles, and Denis Villeneuve (who will be directing the next Bond film).

Normally the James Bond persona subsumes the actor… the actor becomes Bond and always remains Bond, no matter what else he does. But Pattinson is so well-known already for his esoteric roles and big-budget blockbuster starring turns, and he himself has played so many famous characters, that this time (for the first time, I dare say), it’s the other way around.

Ben Roberts, the CEO of the British Film Institute (BFI), noted this, remarking, “He’s a different kind of choice… he comes to the table with a huge amount of baggage, adding that the “amazing thing about Robert Pattinson is his ability to be a chameleon in his roles.”

Personally, I think Pattinson is an extraordinarily skilled performer, one who manages to put a creative and memorable take on even the most generic or hard-worn characters. He’s certainly one of the best actors of his generation. I’m sure that he will be a fabulous Bond, even though I am admittedly surprised by the decision. Pattinson won’t let us down, that I know.

Well, this news also means that Matt Reeves’s sequel to his noirish 2022 masterpiece The Batman, titled The Batman: Part II, will probably be the end of that Batman series. I (and others) cannot imagine Pattinson doing a whole Batman performance in between James Bond performances. But… who knows? He’s a wild guy.

Still, Bond is a very demanding role. Just look at what poor Daniel Craig suffered through!

Pattinson was chosen over Nicholas Hoult, Jack Lowden, Josh O’Connor and Callum Turner. The five actors underwent screen tests in London in late October. The auditions involved stunts, dialogue and camera presence; they were overseen by Nina Gold, an Oscar-nominated (“Hamnet”) and Emmy-winning (“Game of Thrones”) casting director. Bond auditions can be revealing: Henry Cavill, who lost the role to Craig in the previous casting search, told Men’s Health in 2019 that he was asked to re-enact a scene in which Sean Connery’s Bond emerged from a bathroom in nothing but a towel.

Notably, however, this is the first James Bond film that will proceed without the famed Broccoli family/EON productions at the helm, ending their six-decade-long stewardship of the brand. In 2022, the tech giant Amazon acquired 50 percent control over the Bond property as part of its 2022 purchase of MGM (for $8.5 billion). Barbara Broccoli and her half-brother Michael G. Wilson, who inherited the rights from her father Albert R. “Cubby” Broccoli upon his passing in 1996, had retained the other 50 percent, and had been guaranteed a final say on virtually everything. They had “ironclad creative control, deciding when to make a new Bond film, who should play the title role and whether remakes and television spinoffs got made” and “also had final say over every line of dialogue, every casting decision, every stunt sequence, every marketing tie-in, as well as every TV ad, poster and billboard.”

But in February 2025, after reported longstanding creative tensions between Barbara and Amazon, Barbara agreed to transfer creative control to Amazon. Wilson and Broccoli have chosen more passive roles. They will remain co-owners of the franchise, but are relinquishing all creative control to Amazon. In March 2025, it was announced that Harry Potter producer David Heyman would be in charge of the Bond property for Amazon, along with Amy Pascal. Their companies Heyday Films and Pascal Pictures, would produce the future Bond installments.

Almost nothing else is known about this next Bond film, except that the screenplay will be an original story (as there are no more of Ian Fleming’s Bond stories to adapt), written by Steven Knight, the creator of the series Peaky Blinders.

Stay tuned for more updates… and in the meantime, congratulations to Robert Pattinson! Cheers!

Olivia Rutigliano is an Editor at Lit Hub and CrimeReads. #7646. Why the American West Is the Perfect Setting for a Crime Novel

Before we can answer the question of why the American West is the perfect place for a crime story, we need to clarify what the American West is. This is necessary because there seems to be a great deal of confusion on the subject. You can see this in almost any man-on-the-street interview which quickly reveals that the average American’s understanding of geography is less a body of knowledge than it is a collection of strangely confident opinions. For instance, people who live where I do, in Nevada, might look at Boston, New York, Philadelphia, Baltimore, and Washington and think, “You people are practically sharing a driveway.” Similarly, many people who live along the Eastern Seaboard believe that anything west of the Mississippi River qualifies as the West.

For purposes of crime fiction, I propose that the American West should be considered any place that meets all five of the following criteria:

(1) It’s a Place Where Nobody Can Hear You Scream

I’m not kidding. The West has a lot of empty space. In Tallahassee or Atlanta, if someone screams at 2:17 a.m., seventeen people call 911. In Nevada, there may not be another person within 47 miles. This is both atmospheric and convenient for murder. And for crime authors. The amount of open space is incomprehensible to people who live in tighter confines and where the horizon often consists of a strip mall, a water tower and a billboard advertising personal injury attorneys.

Now, don’t get me wrong. There are a lot of desolate areas out here. But while there might not be any humans within earshot of your scream, rest assured the coyotes, wolves, bears, and other high school mascots can hear you. When you scream in the West, be careful, lest you inadvertently ring the dinner bell for some other kind of serial killer.

(2) It’s a Place Where You Can Hide a Body Almost Anywhere

When human remains are discovered in urban areas, there’s a good chance they’ve haven’t been hidden for more than ten minutes. That’s because there’s no good place to dispose of them without being caught on someone’s cell phone video. If you hope to hide your victim, you have to have a space in grandma’s wall or have a large, airtight cooler. In the West, you have deserts and mountains, some with places where no human has ever left a track. You have canyons so vast that the chances of finding a body begin to depend more on plate tectonics than police work. You have ghost towns with mine shafts so deep that any body placed in one will have to be carbon-dated if and when it’s ever found.

(3) It’s a Place Where Everyone Has a Truck

This solves an enormous number of plot problems for western crime authors. Need to transport a body? Truck. Need to follow someone into the wilderness? Truck. Need your protagonist to spend three chapters driving while contemplating the meaning of life? Truck.

Why does everyone in the American West have a truck, you ask? Because daily life demands one. Just watch any of those YouTube channels featuring people who camp in places a normal vehicle could never get to. I’m convinced many of these YouTube campers are serial killers. Also, in a lot of places, there are so few people that everybody knows everybody, so any crime committed has to be hidden where the eyes of prying neighbors aren’t focused. To get there, you need a truck. Trust me.

(4) It’s a Place Where Everyone Owns a Gun

As a writer of crime fiction, this is particularly useful because you can eliminate several pages of explanation.

In the American West, there are more guns than there are people. Most people own multiple firearms, and children are introduced to them shortly after learning to walk. Sometimes earlier. You may argue the merits of this…until little Tommy uses that .22 you bought him to shoot the rattlesnake that’s about to bite his sister. If, some years later, Tommy turns that same rifle on a person, well, that’s the makings of a pretty good crime story.

(5) It’s Place That Gives Your Detective Something Beautiful to Look at While Brooding

And this is, perhaps, the most important thing. The West is practically a literary service.

Mountain ranges. Sunsets. Deserts. Snow. Big sky. Canyons.

A detective in the West is never more than a few minutes away from something worth staring at while contemplating a murder, a missing person, a regrettable decision or the general decline of civilization.

Try doing that on the Jersey Turnpike. A detective there walks outside, looks dramatically into the distance and sees a Wawa.

The West gives a crime novelist something even more than just scenery: space. Space for a crime to happen. Space for a secret to survive. Space for a suspect to disappear. Space for a sheriff to chase him. And, most importantly, space for a character to stand on a ridge at sunset and wonder what the hell happened to his life.

For me, geography is everything. It’s as much a character in my novels as my protagonist, Porter Beck. When I build an outline for a new story, I plot the scenery just as I do my character biographies. I plot the time of year, the colors, the smells, the flora and fauna. In some cases – most actually – the physical setting is as much an adversary to Beck as the person he’s trying to stop. It might be snow drifts or wildfires or the relentless summer heat.

It’s the opportunities this landscape provides that make the American West the perfect place to stage a crime novel. Out here, there is room for everything a crime story needs.

BRUCE BORGOS lives and writes from the Nevada desert where he works hard every day to prove his high school guidance counselor had good instincts when he said “You’ll never be an astronaut.” He has a degree in political science which mostly served to dissuade him from a career in law while at the same time tormenting his wife with endless questions about how telephones work. When not writing, you can usually find him at the local wine store. He is the author of The Bitter Past.

#7645. Lindsay Clancy loses bid to dismiss murder case with retrial possibility

Lindsay Clancy was being tried for first-degree murder. She admitted to killing her three children and claimed that she suffered from postpartum psychosis. (Photo by CJ Gunther/The Boston Herald via the Associated Press)

Lindsay Clancy, a former labor and delivery nurse charged with strangling and killing her three small children in 2023, lost her bid to have her case dismissed Monday, setting the stage for a possible retrial.

Massachusetts Superior Court Judge William Sullivan’s 17-page ruling found that a retrial would not be considered double jeopardy because Clancy’s initial jury was deadlocked.

Clancy, 36, was on trial earlier this year for the strangling deaths of her three young children. The case ended in a mistrial after one juror, known as “Juror Doe,” held out for a conviction. Clancy pleaded not guilty by reason of insanity, alleging that she was going through postpartum psychosis at the time of the tragedy, according to coverage on Courthouse News Service.

Last week, a hearing seeking dismissal of the case explored the role of Michael Desronvil, who is referred to as “Juror Doe” in court records. Desronvil was accused of not following the court’s instructions.

Sullivan found that the evidence “did not reasonably suggest Juror Doe’s inability to deliberate or refusal to follow the law.”

On Nov. 2, the prosecution said it intends to try Clancy again. She initially faced three counts of murder for the deaths of Cora, 5; Dawson, 3; and Callan, 8 months.

#7643. Rhys Bowen on writing real people and settings in historical fiction

One of the aspects of the Royal Spyness series that readers like is that it involves the British royal family in the 1930s. The Prince of Wales, Mrs. Simpson the king and queen, the little princesses walk across the pages and are part of the plots. Other well-known real characters also are featured: Coco Chanel in a couple of books, Noel Coward in several and even Agatha Christie helps solve a mystery in From Cradle to Grave. My fictional heroine is supposedly related to the royals, a great granddaughter of Queen Victoria and thus a cousin first cousin once removed to the Prince of Wales.

Introducing real people to my plots is a bit of a risk, I suppose, but I am by no means unique. Shakespeare certainly wrote about plenty of real people but he retold their true lives. Taking a real person and putting them into a fictional plot is a little different. It is stretching truth and not everybody will be happy with that.

When I started the series I had to think how far I wanted to go from what we know of these characters and I decided I wanted to keep as close as possible to what I knew they said and felt. Queen Mary was a stickler for rules and passionate about antiques so in one plot I had her charge my heroine with reclaiming an antique that had been stolen from her.

I suppose the one person I took the most liberties with was Mrs. Simpson. Since I knew she had a sharp tongue and could be very cruel I enjoyed making her quite unpleasant for several books until she ends up helping my heroine.

Using real people and real settings requires a lot of research. I have to confess that I have poked into every corner of Buckingham Palace, and Kensington Palace, read all the biographies of Chanel and Noel Coward, the Prince of Wales and Mrs Simpson. To me it is important to recreate a real person as faithfully as possible.

In writing about real people each author has to decide how far they want to go and in what ways they might deviate from truth.  Some writers have taken real people and made them sleuths. Stephanie Baron made Jane Austen (very successfully) into a sleuth. Karen Harper had  Queen Elizabeth I solve crimes. Gyles Brandreth makes Oscar Wilde a detective.

Did any of these people really have time to do a little detecting on the side? And without being observed? Jane Austen clearly could have been a good sleuth with her powers of observation of the human condition, especially as she would have been overlooked, sitting in a corner as an unmarried woman. But Queen Elizabeth was accompanied every second of the day.  Could she have found time and opportunity to sleuth a little?

So is the writer allowed to take real people and make them do things they didn’t do? Is there a chance of getting sued? Apparently not if they were a public figure. I could include Agatha Christie in my book, doing what she did best…solve a crime. But I don’t know about making them do something they would never have done: make them a murderer? I think the family would have cause to bring a lawsuit if a respectable person was defamed.

I don’t think I would be comfortable with making a real person do things I know they didn’t do. In fact it gives me great pleasure in having real characters say things I knew they really said. It’s like weaving reality and fiction together.

My favorite example is when Lady Georgie meets her cousins Princess Elizabeth and Princess Margaret. Margaret is three at the time. Georgie says “Hello Margaret,” and Margaret replies, “You have to say Princess Margaret because I’m a princess.” To this Georgie says, “Then you have to say Lady Georgie to me because I’m a lady.”

Margaret looks up at her governess and asks, “Is a lady better than a princess?” To which her governess replies, “One hopes a princess will grow up to be a lady.” True story!

For me the appeal of using real characters and putting my fictional heroine into a real world is that it immediately gives her credibility. It justifies her existence. She’s moving through a real society so we now believe she is real. We know all about Edward VIII and Mrs Simpson and we see Lady Georgie interacting with them. So we accept Lady Georgie as real. Very satisfying.

As well as involving real people in my stories I have introduced real events. We were at Sandringham for the last days of King George V. We were with Mrs Simpson when the king decided to abdicate.

In this latest book in the Royal Spyness series, To Crown It All (book twenty!) the whole story centers around a real event: the coronation of King George and Queen Elizabeth in 1937. This was a well-documented event,  It was even filmed. So I made sure I kept every element completely accurate (except for a minor detail of a plot nobody knew about…which might have happened).

I reasoned that my heroine, Lady Georgie, who is the king’s cousin, would be invited to the Abbey and be involved in the coronation, but I didn’t expect her to get so very involved!

I find it very satisfying to recreate real history, to take readers back to a real time and place, but with the slight addition of my fictional sleuth.

Rhys Bowen is the New York Times bestselling author of more than sixty novels, including Mrs. Endicott’s Splendid Adventure, The Rose Arbor, The Paris Assignment, Where the Sky Begins, The Venice Sketchbook, Above the Bay of Angels, The Victory Garden, The Tuscan Child, and In Farleigh Field, the winner of the Lefty Award for Best Historical Mystery Novel and the Agatha Award for Best Historical Novel. Bowen’s work has won sixteen honors to date, including multiple Agatha, Anthony, and Macavity Awards. Her books have been translated into many languages, and she has fans around the world, including more than seventy thousand Facebook followers. A transplanted Brit, Bowen divides her time between California and Arizona. For more information, visit www.rhysbowen.com.

#7640. 7 mysteries that focus on the motive behind crimes

Means, motive, opportunity: they comprise the classic triad of mystery fiction. Of the three features, I appreciate motive as the real heart of a mystery story.

For two decades before I wrote my debut novel, On the Killer’s Trail, I worked in education and libraries. Prior to that, I was a psychology major and a social worker. I have always been fascinated by what makes people tick. While the success of a work of fiction in any genre may depend on the specifics, for me, its true value lies in the universal truths about human experience that it portrays and reveals. In Louise Penny’s words, “crime was deeply human.”

Here are seven novels that focus on motive in a variety of ways.

No one weaves a mystery from its three strands better than the grande dame of crime fiction, Agatha Christie. In Five Little Pigs, a young woman asks Hercule Poirot to investigate the death of her father for which her mother was convicted sixteen years earlier. The evidence at trial was overwhelming and the accused woman’s defense weak.

Shortly before her own death, the mother professed her innocence to her child in a letter. Due to the passage of time, Poirot must depend on character, rather than evidence, to solve the case. He says, “[Character] is the principal interest of all my cases.” The “five little pigs” are the five people, other than the wife, who had the opportunity to kill Amyas Crane, a talented but eminently unlikeable painter.

Initially, none of the five appears to have a motive to murder him. Poirot tells one of the suspects, “the reason for murder is nearly always to be found by a study of the person murdered.” As Poirot delves into the past, he uncovers the truth about Crane’s life and learns that each of the five did, indeed, have a motive. His analysis of the behavior and motivations of several of the suspects ultimately leads him to the solution.

More than sixty years after Christie’s novel was published, Louise Penny introduces another wise Francophone inspector, Armande Gamache. He, too, investigates the murder of an artist.

The puzzle in Still Life is that, unlike Christie’s victim, Jane Neal of the idyllic Quebecois village of Three Pines was beloved by all. When Neal’s body is found in the woods, felled by an arrow, on Thanksgiving morning, Gamage asks, “who would want to kill kindness?” He later explains “most premeditated murders were about rancid emotions, greed, jealousy, fear, all repressed.”

Penny introduces us to a host of Three Pines villagers, among whom are both suspects and others who will become fond recurring characters in future books, the twenty-first of which was just published this fall.

Sal, a lonely sixth-grade boy, discovers the burned body of middle-school teacher Adam Merkel in the Nevada desert. Merkel had befriended the traumatized boy who came to live on a nearby ranch with his reclusive uncles after the death of his mother.

When one of Adam’s colleagues, who is dealing with her own personal issues, takes it upon herself to investigate, she uncovers secrets in Adam’s past as she also senses that Sal knows more about Adam’s death than he will admit. Her consideration of possible motives explores how the past and present are immutably intertwined.

Sixteen-year-old Lydia Lee has gone missing. When her body is found in a local lake, her devastated parents need to know how and why it happened. Was it a drowning accident, suicide, or foul play?

While this moving novel is not a mystery in the traditional sense, it is an exquisite portrayal of how we are shaped by our families and our experiences and how our motives and actions arise from them. As the family’s emotions and secrets long held in silence are slowly and painfully brought to light, we learn the secrets that Lydia, her siblings, her parents, and their parents have harbored, which ultimately reveal Lydia’s fate.

This historical legal mystery is set in a small town in 1946 Mississippi. Pete Banning is an upright, church-going model citizen and World War II hero. After returning from the Philippines and the horrors of his war experience there, he hopes to resume the life he left behind with his wife Liza and their children on their cotton farm. When he has Liza committed to a psychiatric hospital and, soon after, calmly shoots his pastor and friend, Dexter Belland, Banning refuses to defend himself, stating only, “I have nothing to say.”

Inspired by an actual case from the 1930’s in which the defendant made the same statement until his execution, Grisham keeps the reader guessing until the end why Banning is prepared to die, rather than reveal his motive.

A murder mystery within a murder mystery. Editor Susan Ryeland receives the manuscript of her client, author Alan Conway’s latest mystery novel featuring detective Atticus Pund, but with the story’s ending missing.

When Conway is found dead, Ryeland concludes that the manuscript involves real-life events and that Conway’s murderer stole the final pages to avoid incrimination. Ryeland sets out to find the motive and perpetrator of Pund’s fictional mystery to find Conway’s real-life killer.

Stuart Turton, The 7 ½ Deaths of Evelyn Hardcastle

Straddling genres, this mystery borrows from speculative fiction to shift time and perspective as the protagonist investigates a murder from the viewpoints of multiple characters within the setting of a classic English country estate. Aiden Bishop wakes up at Blackheath Manor with amnesia and no knowledge of why he is there.

In each of eight days in a time loop, he finds himself inhabiting a different guest at the manor until he can solve the murder of the young heiress of the estate, Evelyn Hardcastle, who died that evening. If he cannot solve the case by the end of day eight, he is doomed to repeat the cycle with his memory wiped clean.

Whatever the setting or sub-genre, the key to a murder mystery is motive. As Inspector Armande Gamage put it, “My job is to find people who take lives. And to do that, I have to find out why.”

Alice Openshaw has been a fan of mysteries since the age of ten, when she discovered Perry Mason books at her tiny town’s public library. She holds a BA in psychology from Middlebury College in Vermont and an MLS from Vanderbilt University. She lived in rural Maine for thirty years, where she worked as a librarian and adult literacy teacher and raised three children and an assortment of animals on a small farm. She now lives near Cape Cod, Massachusetts, with her husband and her tuxedo cat, Frankie. On the Killer's Trail is her debut novel.

#7639. What happened at Weil Gotshal? Could tech help other firms avoid that fate?

November 11, 2026, 9:17 am CST By Victor Li

There have been plenty of law firm failures over the years. For instance, there was a run on closures thanks to the Great Recession, and Dewey & LeBoeuf’s 2012 failure sent shockwaves throughout the industry.

But when Weil, Gotshal & Manges announced last month that it would be winding down operations, it felt different compared to the others before.

After all, many of the BigLaw firms that went out of the business during the Great Recession had been overexposed in certain areas, and when the housing market crashed, so did their business. Dewey’s failure happened for a lot of reasons, mainly due to big money guarantees to partners, an ill-advised merger, and alleged financial irregularities that resulted in criminal indictments.

Weil Gotshal, though, had long been a firm with one of the best reputations on Wall Street, let alone the world. How did a firm like that end up joining the others on the dustheap? And could technology play a role in helping other firms avoid such a fate in the future?

In this episode of the Legal Rebels Podcast, Noah Waisberg talks to the ABA Journal’s Victor Li about those and other topics. Waisberg is the co-founder and the CEO of Zuva—an artificial intelligence contract analysis platform—and a longtime advocate of using technology to review contracts. He’s also a former Weil Gotshal associate, having worked there as a summer associate in 2005 and then as an associate from 2006 to 2010.

Rivals race to rescue Weil Gotshal lawyers as firm heads toward closure

#7638. Catherine Townsend on treating dating like detective work, and vice versa

When I was a dating columnist for The Independent in London, I would often point out the similarities between dating and detective work. I’d flag that in both scenarios, you find yourself sitting in front of a stranger—the difference being that in a potential love match, the skeletons in their closet are (hopefully) merely metaphorical, rather than decomposing in a crawl space.

The same logic works in reverse. Conducting investigative interviews is, in crucial ways, very much like being on one long and strange first date. The idea is to ask open-ended questions and to encourage the person you are trying to get information from to keep talking about themselves. If they keep talking, eventually you can find the inconsistencies in their story.

A more cynical take would be that falling in love is like one long con. When we like someone, our brain is wired to look for commonalities. And the more we like someone, the more we mimic their behavior. This works extremely well for getting someone to trust you— and that is why con artists mimic our movements, too, for less pure reasons.

But my job when I’m conducting an interview is to see the worst in people.

In 2010, I was living in Los Angeles, had just enrolled in PI school with Dale, and was moonlighting as a PI. State boards give credit to-ward investigative hours for police work, which is why retired police detectives can qualify as licensed private investigators. But, despite the fact that investigative journalism uses a lot of the same skill sets as detective work, journalists are given zero credit for hours worked in newsrooms.

My first encounters with law enforcement had been less than satisfactory, and I was convinced that this was because, for the most part, they didn’t trust the media. So I wanted to get some more specialized training, something that would raise my skill levels and, hopefully, my esteem in the eyes of the police departments that I was trying to sweet-talk.

Living in Los Angeles, the quintessential sunny place for shady people, is like having permanent residence inside a noir mystery painted with the rainbow neon sunsets, and traffic jams, of Grand Theft Auto V.

Dale sent me out on a lot of matrimonial surveillances, and they almost always unfolded in the same way.

Sometimes, the clients would summon me to their homes. But, following the detective manual logic on interrogations, I preferred to coax the clients into nonthreatening, neutral territory—preferably one that invoked feelings of nostalgia. I found that magic location sliding into a red leatherette booth at Bob’s Big Boy diner in Burbank at sunrise, sipping a ten-ounce mug of Big Boy medium roast, and watching the pink clouds float across an impossibly bright, Monet-meets-vaporwave California sky.

After that, things usually get complicated. The client asks me to follow their boyfriend/husband/girlfriend/married boyfriend who also has another girlfriend but has promised that they are his only mistress. (I pretend to ignore the logical fallacies of that argument.) I ask them what they hope to accomplish from a surveillance.

I’m honest: I’ll tell them that it’s expensive, uncertain, and a hell of a lot harder than it looks on TV. (If you don’t believe me, try identifying a subject described as “white man in a suit” outside a downtown office building at night from a fuzzy Facebook photo. Bonus points if it’s a rainy winter night and only a few inches of skin are visible!)

I’ll also ask them why they believe that their loved one has been unfaithful, and often they will tell me something that lets me know that they already know the truth: Maybe they have found a topless selfie of his secretary, or a scrap of lacy women’s underwear in the glove compartment of his Prius.

I try to always have these conversations over something sweet, which is why I prefer to meet at restaurants. I load the table with strawberry waffles or a banana milkshake with extra maraschino cherries, since bad news goes down easier with a heavy dose of sugar lubricant. Even Cinnabon at the mall food court is better than nothing: Studies show that our animal brains associate the smells of cinnamon and vanilla with comfort and security.

“Well, it sounds like you already know the answer,” I inevitably say. Why would you think that this is a good person, despite mounting evidence to the contrary?

Before I dig in and disrupt lives, potentially unearthing a truth that could shake the foundations of a person’s existence, I always ask the same question: Do you really want to know? Little white lies can be the glue that holds relationships together. No, you don’t look fat in those white jeans. Yes, you’re the best sex I’ve ever had.

I make a point of sliding one of my Patrick Bateman-style thick business cards across the table and making a reference to The Matrix: Would they rather take the blue pill and remain blissfully ignorant, or the red pill to see where the rabbit hole, however unpleasant, leads?

Some people have a compulsive need to know the reality, however brutal and disruptive it will be to their existence, and they will continue to pick it apart like an overeager esthetician digging out blackheads on YouTube. And then there are those who decide that for whatever reason—long marriage, double mortgage, social hierarchy, or something else—they want to stay inside the much happier bubble they have created.

Before you ask a question that could shatter your reality forever, it’s important to know which camp you fall into. Because once the bubble is pierced, it’s almost impossible to get back in—and if a person chooses to overlook a betrayal, an infidelity, or something worse, lying to themselves afterward can become a full-time job.

Catherine Townsend is a journalist, private investigator, and podcaster. She is the host of the iHeartMedia podcast Hell and Gone and Red Collar. After beginning her career as a staff writer for New York Magazine, Catherine moved to London to create The Independent’s very popular “Sleeping Around” dating column. Her articles have appeared in publications including The Atlantic, Elle, New York, GQ, Marie Claire, Cosmopolitan, The Daily Mail, The New York Post, Investigation Discovery, and HuffPost. She became a licensed private investigator in 2013. She is the author of How to Survive a Murder Investigation: A True Story of Death and Danger in the Ozarks.

#7637. Cutting the deadwood with Clive Cussler – my Dad

When the opportunity arose to co-write with Clive Cussler, I thought it would be a uniquely fun experience. After all, he was my father.

I knew Clive as a genial, good-natured man who loved a good laugh. He was the type of person who expected a lot from himself, but not from others. Growing up, I had ducked household chores as a kid, crashed the family car as a teen, and frittered away college tuition money on pizza and beer, all without incurring any lasting parental disdain. I expected our collaboration on adventure stories to be equally lighthearted and unruffled.

And so it was– until I submitted an early chapter in our first book together. I had written a scene in which our protagonist, Dirk Pitt, was beaten to a bloody pulp by a nefarious villain. I had crossed a line with Clive’s protagonist, and the curtain of joviality suddenly came crashing down. It was then and there that I realized the man who didn’t take life at all seriously was dead serious about his writing. Clive knew exactly how he wanted his adventure stories crafted, and he was uncompromising about their execution.

It took me back to when I was six years old, and my father began writing at night and on weekends in my childhood bedroom, which also served as the family den. He had stacks of paperback books on his desk by the likes of Hammond Innes, Donald Hamilton, and Alistair MacLean. Key passages and sections of dialogue were carefully underlined as he studied the contemporary masters of adventure writing like a Rhodes scholar.

Clive brought that same dedication to research into his own stories. He loved history, and early on began incorporating historical hooks as key elements in his books. But he never made these inclusions lightly; they were always thoroughly researched.

In the prologue to Treasure, a Roman legion is attacked by frontier barbarians in 391 A.D. The legionnaires are supported by an historically accurate contingent of Syrian archers and armed with laminated oval shields unique to that particular era of fading Roman dominance. His descriptions of the weaponry, military organization, and battle tactics demonstrated an impressive depth of study.

I was a young teen when Clive wrote his breakout bestseller, Raise the Titanic! He threw himself into researching the Titanic, borrowing every library book he could find on the ship. He joined the Titanic Historical Society to obtain its quarterly journals and enlisted me to stay up with him to watch the British production of A Night to Remember on late-night television. Such was his devotion to the topic that when he purchased and built a Revell plastic model of the ship, he manually extended the lengths of the funnels when he discovered they weren’t properly to scale. The joy he took in his research was reflected in his fictional raising of the grand ship and having it complete its maiden voyage to New York.

I share his passion for research, finding it one of the more rewarding aspects of writing. We often discussed the delicate balance involved in incorporating detailed research into a story. Knowledge of the fine details and nuances of a subject can add great flavor to a scene, but there’s also a risk of information overload. As writers, we become mini-experts on a topic and feel compelled to share our newfound knowledge. One common pitfall involves describing places we’ve visited. A writer on vacation in Dublin might later incorporate a night at a pub into a chapter scene. Eager to share the experience, she spends two pages describing the weathered wooden floor, the dusty bottles of whiskey lined above the bar, and the clover designs of the cardboard drink coasters on the tables. An atmospheric plunge suddenly turns into a boring travelogue.

Those of us who co-wrote with Clive were more than familiar with the crossed-out manuscript pages he would return to us when we got carried away with our own exuberant descriptions.

“Cut out the deadwood,” he would implore. “Make it fly.”

Clive always wanted to drive the narrative forward, but he wasn’t averse to expounding in detail at important points in the story. He might explain an ancient mystery in depth, such as the history of Troy and its related archaeological excavations in Trojan Odyssey. Or he might dive deep into describing an advanced technology incorporated into the story. These passages weren’t intended to demonstrate his knowledge, but to educate readers about elements that ultimately mattered to the plot.

Clive was a product of his time, and that also influenced his outlook on pacing and structure. Going to the movies was a ritual in his childhood, and he religiously attended matinees every Saturday afternoon. The main features were preceded by short movie serials, such as The Hurricane Express, which starred a young John Wayne. I know this because a local Denver television station aired the episodes in the 1970s, and my father watched them every week with a bowl of popcorn, as if he were eight years old again. Each episode was less than twenty minutes long, requiring a quick setup, an action sequence or two, and, of course, an ending cliffhanger. He wrote with that same sort of pacing and visual storytelling in mind. Clive especially relished ending a chapter with a cliffhanger, keeping readers eager to turn the page.

Ultimately, it was the swashbuckling sense of fun those films imparted that most influenced his approach to writing. He was more interested in entertaining readers than impressing them with his prose, and entertainment always took precedence. Clive wanted his stories to be gripping and fast-paced, of course, but the key ingredient may have been the very quality that defined his own character: a genuine sense of fun.

Dirk Cussler is the author of Clive Cussler's The Devil's Sea, and coauthor with Clive Cussler of eight previous Dirk Pitt adventures: Black Wind, Treasure of Khan, Arctic Drift, Crescent Dawn, Poseidon's Arrow, Havana Storm, Odessa Sea, and Celtic Empire. He serves as president of NUMA, where he continues his father's legacy of searching for important historical shipwrecks. He lives in Connecticut.

#7636. Elly Griffiths’ 5 favorite female detectives in fiction

Women have always solved crimes. I’m sure Eve knew immediately who killed Abel, although admittedly there was only one suspect. Grendel’s mother, in Beowulf, is one of the greatest justice-seekers in literature. The Wife of Bath would make a formidable sleuth, specializing in domestic cases.

It was some time, though, before crime-solving women appeared in print. In The Female Detective by Andrew Forrester (the pseudonym of James Redding Ware), published in 1864, Mrs Gladden is thought to be a dressmaker but is, in fact, a detective. The Revelations of a Lady Detective by William Hayward, also published in 1864, features Mrs Paschall, recruited by the Chief of Police to form a squad of women officers. In Mr Bazalgette’s Agent by Leonard Merrick, published in 1888, Miriam Lea is an aristocrat who becomes a private eye after falling on hard times.

Interestingly, these first women sleuths were professionals, in that they earned their living from detection. The era of the talented but overlooked amateur, exemplified by Miss Marple, comes later.

When I created forensic archaeologist Dr Ruth Galloway, I was drawing on the tradition of the civilian expert, often a woman, who assists the police. There many great unofficial detectives in modern crime fiction;  Freida Klein in Nicki French’s books, for example, or Rhona Macleod in Lin Anderson’s series. There are also many terrific women police officers: Val McDermid’s Karen Pirie, Sarah Hilary’s Marnie Rome, Nadine Matheson’s Anjelica Henley,  Jane Casey’s Maeve Kerrigan.

Here are five of my favorite female detectives, official or otherwise.

She’s not, strictly speaking, a detective but Marian Halcombe in The Woman in White by Wilkie Collins, is surely one of the greatest sleuths in crime fiction. Laura Fairlie is ostensibly the heroine but Marian, clever, brave and intrepid, is the beating heart of the book.

The Woman in White, published in 1859/60, is known as one of the great “sensation novels” and the sweeping narrative includes abduction, organized crime and murder. One of the most thrilling scenes has Marian clambering over rooftops at night in order to overhear a conversation between the villains Percival Glyde and Count Fosco. She’s in her petticoat because her voluminous silk skirt would have rustled too much. No wonder even evil Fosco is more than half in love with her.

No list would be complete without Agatha Christie’s famous spinster sleuth. Jane Marple was apparently inspired by the many unmarried women after the first world war, who, as they grew older, were often ignored by the world around them.

Miss Marple, poised with rose clippers in her garden or bent over her crochet, makes the most of her invisibility. Almost every crime reminds Miss Marple of something she saw in her home village of St Mary Mead. She’s caustic, quietly brilliant and ruthless when on the trail of a murderer. In A Caribbean Mystery Jason Rafiel describes her as “Nemesis in a pink shawl.” Miss Marple is also surprisingly well-travelled, helped by a generous nephew and a doctor who is always happy to prescribe a holiday.

I was delighted to be asked to contribute to Marple, a new collection of short stories featuring the divine Miss M. It was a daunting task made easier by the fact that we all think we know Miss Marple but she can still always surprise us.

Ann Cleeves meant The Crow Trap to be a standalone novel. She was as surprised as anyone when, after a death at an isolated cottage in the Pennines, a rather unusual detective arrives to solve the case.

DI Vera Stanhope is “a large woman, amply covered” with a bulbous nose, man-sized feet and pitted skin. She’s scruffily dressed and carries a plastic bag containing her notes. She’s also brilliant, unconventional and frighteningly forthright. There are now thirteen Vera novels with a fourteenth, rumored to be the last, scheduled for 2027.

The TV series Vera, starring Brenda Blethyn as the eponymous detective, has run for fourteen seasons.  Through the years we have learnt more about Vera’s history and her deep connection to the Northumbrian countryside but we can never second-guess our heroine who, like the similarly disheveled Columbo, always has the last word.

Nancy Spain wrote six fantastically funny and atmospheric crime novels starring the indomitable Miriam Birdseye. I’m sure she would have gone on to write more if she hadn’t been killed in a  plane crash at the untimely age of forty-six. But in Miriam, Nancy has given us a detective for all time.

Miriam is a  wildly glamorous “vaudeville star” whose modus operandi seems to be to get engaged to the prime suspect as quickly as possible. Miriam’s sidekick is the Russian ballerina, Natasha Nevkorina, whose ambition is to do as little as possible. Miriam is always prepared to dress up in the name of detection.  Was there ever a better chapter heading than this, in Cinderella Goes to the Morgue–Enter Miriam, Disguised as a Principal Boy?

Susie Steiner also left us tragically early, dying of a brain tumor in 2022. She only wrote three novels featuring DS Manon Bradshaw but she created one of my favorite modern detectives.

Manon, named after the operatic heroine, is a terrific character: clever, kind, funny and often frustratingly stubborn. Manon’s relationships with her colleagues, Davy and Harriet, and, especially, with her adopted son, Fly, are beautifully described; full of warmth, nuance and humour. I’m sorry that there aren’t more novels about Manon, but this trilogy is crime-writing perfection.

Stella Darnell first appears in The Detective’s Daughter by Lesley Thomson. Stella is the daughter of a police officer who died before he could solve his most important case. Stella had a complicated relationship with her father and has taken another path; she’s a cleaner.

Through the course of ten intricately-plotted books, Lesley Thomson charts how Stella, reluctantly at first, becomes a private detective whilst running her own cleaning agency. She solves crimes “stain by stain.” Along the way, Stella acquires a wonderful collection of assistants, including Jack Harmon, a tube driver who can sense murder….

Elly Griffiths is the author of the Ruth Galloway and Brighton mystery series, as well as the standalone novels The Stranger Diaries, winner of the Edgar Award for Best Novel; The Postscript Murders; and Bleeding Heart Yard. She is the recipient of the CWA Dagger in the Library Award and the Mary Higgins Clark Award. She lives in Brighton, England.

#7635. Judicial Watch founder Larry Klayman disbarred by Supreme Court

The U.S. Supreme Court disbarred conservative watchdog group Judicial Watch founder and activist Larry Klayman on Monday following his 18-month suspension issued last year by the District of Columbia Court of Appeals. (Image from Shutterstock)

The U.S. Supreme Court disbarred conservative watchdog group Judicial Watch founder and activist Larry Klayman on Monday following his 18-month suspension issued last year by the District of Columbia Court of Appeals.

Klayman’s disbarment follows a suspension for violating numerous ethical rules in connection to representing rancher Cliven Bundy in Nevada federal court, Law360 reports.

Bundy had been facing a criminal case over his 2014 standoff with federal agents when Klayman, a Florida attorney, sought pro hac vice status to join Bundy’s legal team in 2016. The District of Columbia Office of Disciplinary Counsel filed a complaint against Klayman in 2018, claiming that he misled the U.S. District Court for the District of Nevada about his disciplinary status when he tried to represent Bundy. A D.C. appellate court ruling adopted the District of Columbia Bar’s findings and suspension.

The disciplinary office alleged that Klayman also made baseless claims against the judge who denied his admission to the Nevada court.

Klayman, in a statement to Law360 on Monday said, “The order contains no factual or legal reasoning, is subject to reconsideration and is not final. I made a compelling submission to the Supreme Court recently, and apparently, it was not considered. This will be a basis for reconsideration.”

#7634. Christina Henry on translating the unexpected horrors of motherhood into fiction

We all have a picture in our head of a mother—what we think a mother should be or shouldn’t be, what ideal motherhood looks like. Society creates expectations for mothers, and mothers who color outside those lines are often censured by those around them.

But being a mother, or a stepmother, or a mother figure, is hard. If you carry a child you might think that pregnancy will be nine months of glowing, radiant bliss (that’s what all those parenting influencers say on TikTok, don’t they?) Instead, you’re coping with swollen feet and sciatica, and the constant worry that you might do something that will accidentally harm your growing baby.

Once your child is born you might think, Great, it’s going to be nothing but sunshine and roses from here on out. But parenting isn’t just drippy ice cream cones on the beach and smiling while riding carousels. There are so many things you can’t anticipate—unexpected illnesses, trouble at school, headstrong kids who simply want their own way.

The truth of the matter that having a child and raising a child are often some of the most anxiety-riddled years of a person’s life. Even when nothing’s going wrong, a mother can often feel like something just might go wrong. The worry they are feeling is somehow a hedge against bad things happening—parental anxiety as a shield against actual harm.

Fictional mothers, of course, get the worst of it. It’s bad enough that real-world mothers have to cope with spiking fevers and school permission forms and judgmental in-laws. But what if you desperately want a child but it turns out your baby was also, say, the son of Satan? Or what if you love your children with all your heart but you keep hearing things, seeing things that you aren’t sure are actually there? What if the people around you aren’t to be trusted? What if you feel like you can’t trust yourself?

Everyone knows about Rosemary, right? Poor Rosemary Woodhouse, whose gaslighting jerk of a husband, Guy, trades her womb for a successful career.

In Ira Levin’s classic novel of motherhood horror, Rosemary’s Baby, Rosemary is a cheery newlywed who wants to have a child. Guy is a struggling actor who keeps just missing his big break and wants to wait a little longer to start a family. A bit of timely luck allows them to sign a lease in an older building called the Bramford, a place that’s notoriously difficult to get into. Rosemary is thrilled that, at least, she will have the decoration of a new place to keep her busy, but she still wishes for a baby.

An older couple, Roman and Minnie Castavet, live in the next apartment. Rosemary finds them nosy and annoying, but for some reason Guy likes them and starts to visit regularly. Then, a miracle happens. The actor who cast in a role that Guy almost got is suddenly struck blind (a miracle for Guy, of course, not so much for the other actor) and Guy lands a role that can make his career.  Soon after this unexpectedly fortuitous occurrence, he decides that he does, in fact, want a baby.

Shortly after, Rosemary has a terrible dream—a dream about a beast who rapes her while several people look on. And then, the second miracle happens. Rosemary is pregnant. Except her pregnancy doesn’t feel right, and everyone around her keeps telling her it’s fine.

Rosemary’s journey is so harrowing because no matter what she says or does or even knows with absolute certainty, no one will believe her. If you’ve never read this one it’s time to give it a try.

Kit Burgoyne’s The Captive is a clever play on the I’ve-been-impregnated-by-Satan-against-my-will story, or in this case, by an entity alternately referred to as “The Long-Before” or “Him.” An underground revolutionary group that call themselves the Nail decide to kidnap Adeline Woolsaw, the wealthy heiress of a vast network of connected businesses, in hopes of exposing the Woolsaws and their corruption to the public. The only time Adeline ever seems to leave the vast estate where she lives is to go to the doctor’s office, so the group decides to grab her as she leaves her appointment.

Unfortunately for the Nail, Adeline is pregnant. Even more unfortunately, Adeline is going into labor in the van. Just to add to their confusion, Adeline most definitely does not want to return home to her parents. It seems that her parents worship this evil entity and arranged to have Adeline carry His child in order to establish total world domination.

This pitch-black story skewers the cultists, the radical revolutionaries and the oligarchs that run everything equally and mashes it all up into a super-fun (and frequently gory) thriller.

Helen Phillip’s The Need is probably one of my favorite novels of the last ten years. I’ve never read another book that so accurately embodies both the intense love of a mother for her children and also the profound, dragging monotony of the daily tasks that make up her day.

Molly is a mom of two and a paleobotanist, alone with the kids while her partner travels. She is exhausted, exhausted in that bone-deep way parents often are, feeling like she wants to stay on top of everything but she simply cannot.

When she hears footsteps in her home she thinks she’s imagining them. She’s anxious about a potential home invasion. She can’t trust herself. She’s just sleep-deprived. But then she comes face to face with an intruder wearing a mask, and the reality of Molly’s world tilts precariously on its side.

The less you know about this one, the better. It unfolds like a strange and fascinating puzzle box, revealing layers as it goes.

Neena Viel’s debut Listen to Your Sister isn’t about a mother, per se. But it is about Calla Williams, a twenty-five-year-old woman just trying to keep it together, who reluctantly agrees to become the guardian to her sixteen-year-old brother Jamie. Jamie, like most 16-year-olds, is not interested in his sister’s authority, or any kind of authority, really. Their brother Dre agreed to help Calla with Jamie, but he has his own struggles and isn’t exactly present.

Calla keeps trying, keeps sacrificing, keeps muddling along trying to do her best like every mother figure.  Ever since her brothers were young she’s had visions of their dying in horrible ways, and her nightmares stoke her anxiety over their well-being. But her resentment is growing. No matter how much she loves her brothers, they don’t seem to love her enough to change.

One day Jamie’s behavior goes a little too far and the siblings are forced to flee their homes to hide out at a cabin in the woods. It’s there that Calla’s patience finally snaps, and her brothers discover that the nightmares Calla has had all their lives might just be real.

Neena Viel’s writing is so intense, so profoundly visual, that this book has been indelibly imprinted on my brain. I’m still thinking about it months later.

In my own upcoming novel Pinfeathers, stay-at-home mom Nora Pacetti is tired and frustrated that her husband, Adam, isn’t keeping up his end of the parenting bargain. But those problems seem trivial once Nora discovers a strange object sticking out of her baby’s arm.

Nora thinks it must be a splinter. But when she examines it closely the object seems to have come through her daughter’s skin, not pierced it from the outside. Then Nora’s mother Giulia looks at it and renders her verdict—it’s a pinfeather, a baby feather.

Nora doesn’t know what to believe, and then she finds another one. Does her daughter have a strange disease, or is she actually turning into a bird?

Christina Henry is the author of The Mermaid, Lost Boy, Alice, Red Queen, and the national bestselling Black Wings series featuring Agent of Death Madeline Black and her popcorn-loving gargoyle, Beezle.

#7633. Judge removed for engaging in ‘extensive and severe misconduct’

A Los Angeles County Superior Court judge has been removed from his position for making inappropriate racial and sexual comments and several other instances of misconduct. (Photo from Shutterstock)

A Los Angeles County Superior Court judge has been removed from his position for making inappropriate racial and sexual comments and several other instances of misconduct.

In its decision Tuesday, the California Commission on Judicial Performance said Los Angeles County Superior Court Judge Robert Draper “persistently violated the standards governing judicial behavior and engaged in extensive and severe misconduct.” The commission also said the judge failed to accept responsibility or show remorse for his actions.

Among the charges, the commission considered Draper’s conduct during a February 2023 posttrial hearing in a sexual harassment case, where he lectured a Black attorney about Black football players and race relations in the South. It also examined comments that Draper made to female attorneys in the case—while in his chambers—about male attorneys who slept with their secretaries at his prior law firm.

Other charges alleged that Draper made inappropriate comments to a female colleague and a female court personnel, engaged in improper ex parte communications, and improperly disclosed confidential juvenile records.

Draper has said the charges “were contrary to all credible evidence and/or taken wholly out of context.”

An attorney who represented Draper didn’t respond to a request for comment from Courthouse News Service.

#7632. Wells Fargo faces labor board complaint over union vote

The National Labor Relations Board alleged the lender threatened and retaliated against workers in favor of unionization at a California branch.

The National Labor Relations Board has accused Wells Fargo of illegally threatening and retaliating against employees and coercing workers to prevent fair unionization votes at a California branch.

Most employees of an Atwater, California, branch who signed cards supporting unionization in December 2023 voted against unionization the following month, a regional director of the NLRB alleged, in a complaint filed Feb. 11 and seen by Bloomberg,

The NLRB claims Wells Fargo coerced workers to vote against unionization. Wells Fargo has denied that allegation.

The labor board wants the bank to recognize and negotiate with the union despite the vote, based on a 2023 precedent case. The 2023 Cemex ruling strengthened the NLRB's power to compel companies that violate labor laws to recognize unions.

However, Republicans and business groups oppose the precedent. The acting general counsel of NLRB, William Cowen, or his permanent replacement, could withdraw, amend, or settle the Wells Fargo complaint.

President Donald Trump appointed Cowen acting general counsel this month, days after firing NLRB’s previous chief lawyer Jennifer Abruzzo, a Biden appointee, and Democratic board member Gwynne Wilcox.

The email notifying Wilcox of her termination said she was being fired since she did not “share the objectives” of the present administration. Wilcox’s ouster has left the board with only two members coupled with existing vacancies and does not meet the minimum number of members needed to adjudicate routine cases.

Wilcox is suing Trump, alleging the president surpassed his authority in firing her and requesting that she be allowed to resume her work as an NLRB member.

The NLRB complaint does not signify a complete investigation or a full adjudication of the allegations; rather, the regional office found that the allegations may be sufficient to go to a hearing to consider all evidence and make credibility determinations, a Wells Fargo spokesperson noted.

Employees at the Atwater branch voted 3-1 to reject unionization in January 2024. The branch manager allegedly told staff she knew about organizing discussions and warned about camera surveillance. She also reportedly told workers that Wells Fargo would apply stricter work conditions and would make union supporters stay longer hours.

A Wells Fargo spokesperson said the bank trains its managers to respect the rights of its employees to freely associate and join or support a union, or to bargain collectively with a representative of their choosing.

“We train our managers to comply with labor law and respect the rights of our employees,” the spokesperson told Banking Dive via email. “In this case, the majority of eligible employees freely voted against a union in a Board supervised secret ballot election and the facts do not support allegations to the contrary.”

Wells Fargo is cooperating with the investigation but believes these allegations are unfounded and plans to defend the company and employees, the spokesperson added.

An NLRB hearing before a judge is scheduled for October, and Wells Fargo, if ordered to collectively bargain, can appeal to NLRB members in Washington, Bloomberg reported.

Recently, unionized Wells Fargo employees hit a new challenge in organizing. The bank's conduct management intake team won its union vote 21-16 in December, making it the first non-branch unit at Wells Fargo to unionize.

The team, which handles customer and employee complaints across various locations, has now filed an unfair labor practice charge with the NLRB through Wells Fargo Workers United-CWA. The complaint alleges that the bank illegally refuses to engage in collective bargaining following the certified union vote, American Banker reported. However, the bank contends it’s waiting for the outcome of the NLRB’s review and claims there were procedural flaws in the handling of the vote.

CWA unionized 24 Wells Fargo branches last year, with around 200 employees being organized.

Wells Fargo CEO Charlie Scharf pushed back on employee unionization efforts last April, saying it’s important to “make clear that we continue to believe that our employees are best served by working directly with Wells Fargo and our leadership team.”

#7630. Elvis Presley estate shakes up licensing, copyright lawsuit against AI music generator

Rock musician Elvis Presley performs June 27, 1968. (Photo by Michael Ochs Archives/Getty Images)

Rock star Elvis Presley’s estate and music rights holders sued artificial intelligence music generator Suno on Friday in a California court for unlawfully using the entertainer’s name, image and likeness and infringing on copyrighted material.

The plaintiffs, consisting of exclusive rights holders with control of Presley’s music, name, image and copyrighted works, claimed that Suno violated Tennessee’s Ensuring Likeness, Voice and Image Security Act, known as the ELVIS Act. The law is designed to protect performers from unauthorized use of their voices and likeness, which includes AI-generated imitations. The plaintiffs also accused Suno of rampant copyright infringement.

“The name, image, likeness and music of Elvis Presley are among the most valuable intellectual property assets in the world. We protect those rights vigorously,” Lark-Marie Antón, a representative for the plaintiffs, told Courthouse News Service.

In the U.S. District Court for the Northern District of California, the plaintiffs produced numerous exhibits containing nearly 50 recorded examples that they said infringe on Presley’s likeness and their copyrights. They are seeking damages and an injunction to stop Suno from additional infringement of works and are requesting the platform destroy unauthorized copies, including those in datasets.

“We do not allow prompts for specific artists’ names and songs and work with third-party providers to screen uploaded audio files and lyrics for potential misuse. We are always working to strengthen our guardrails, and we will continue to add new safeguards that protect artists and our users,” Suno said in a statement.

#7628. The SEC has requested to delay climate rule arguments. What’s next?

Sustainable investing experts are not surprised by the delay and say it is expected to have minimal immediate impact.

Acting Securities and Exchange Commission Chair Mark Uyeda’s decision last week to ask the Eighth Circuit Court of Appeals to delay arguments for the agency’s climate risk disclosure rule did not come as a surprise to regulatory experts in the space.

While the change is expected to have minimal immediate impact, it sets the stage for a shift in focus for the SEC under the Trump administration.

The SEC issued its long-awaited climate-risk disclosure rule last March, nearly two years after it was first proposed — and amid over 24,000 public comments. Uyeda was one of two commissioners to vote against the rule’s approval. The rule was immediately met with multiple lawsuits that were later consolidated into the Eighth Circuit. The spate of legal challenges led the agency to stay the rule’s implementation in April.

Given the agency’s stay and the change in administration, Tom Willman, regulatory lead for artificial intelligence sustainability platform Clarity AI, said Uyeda’s decision came “as no great surprise.”

“It is nevertheless disappointing that investors will be deprived of much-needed financially material information related to climate related risks,” Willman said by email Wednesday.

Julie Gorte, senior vice president of sustainable investing at Impax Asset Management was more blunt in an interview: “The only person on the planet who didn't see this coming was Rip Van Winkle,” she said Wednesday.

Uyeda’s recommended pullback on defending the SEC climate rule follows his prior critiques of the rule. During the hearing on the final climate rule, in the weeks after it was finalized and in his Feb. 11 statement announcing the delay request, Uyeda maintained his belief that the SEC does not have the authority to promulgate the rule or require such disclosures.

Jenner & Block Partner Jennifer Lee, a former assistant director of the SEC Enforcement Division, said Uyeda’s position is “consistent with the new, Republican-led SEC’s shift back to focusing on ‘bread and butter’ investor disclosure issues.” Lee, who now represents companies and financial institutions in regulatory investigations and litigation, told ESG Dive in emailed comments Thursday that she expects that focus to include an emphasis on materiality, while looking to avoid “overly prescriptive disclosure requirements for public companies.”

The change in SEC posture, however, is expected to have a minimal impact for companies or investors, according to Willman and Gorte.

“The impact of this is going to be extraordinarily minimal, partly because it was never enforced in the first place,” Gorte said Wednesday. “So we never had better climate reporting stimulated by U.S. regulatory postures to begin with. And for U.S. companies, or for any company really, a lot of the big ones are probably still going to have to be reporting on all the same things that were in that rule because of [other jurisdictions].”

Willman echoed that note and said that many U.S. companies already voluntarily report climate risks due to investor demand, in addition to growing regulatory requirements both overseas in jurisdictions like the European Union, and stateside in California. New York recently reintroduced its own version of California’s climate disclosure laws.

Additionally, Stephen O’Day, a partner at Smith, Gambrell & Russell, noted the intervenors in the case could continue the rule’s defense, even though the SEC’s announcement indicates this iteration of the agency is not inclined to defend the rules. In the case of the climate rule, 18 states and the District of Columbia have signed on as intervenors to support the agency’s rule.

O’Day said a similar process happened after intervenors continued the defense for enforcement actions taken by the Clinton-era administration for violations of the Clean Air Act by coal-fired plants. Ultimately, the intervenors prevailed, and the Supreme Court upheld the actions.

“The proceedings pending in the Eighth Circuit involve challenges filed by multiple parties and intervenors, any of which could seek to continue defense of the SEC rules,” O’Day said. “So, while the court may grant the requested 45-day pause, it remains to be seen whether any such pause will result in the end of the SEC’s final rules.”

Regardless, sustainability programs and disclosures are expected to continue.

“Regulatory shifts don’t change the fundamental reality: physical climate risk is already priced into markets,” Lukky Ahmed, CEO of climate risk data and analytics platform Climate X, said by email Wednesday. Firms have a fiduciary responsibility to continue to assess, manage and disclose climate risks to their operations, Ahmed said.

“Integrating climate resilience and adaptation strategies isn’t just prudent — it’s essential for maintaining business performance, driving shareholder returns, and protecting communities," Ahmed said.

Despite the shifting federal policy stance, “there is a lot of faith that the drivers of sustainability remain in place no matter who is in anyone's White House,” Gorte told ESG Dive.

“If we don't solve the climate crisis, there are going to be … parts of the globe that are probably uninhabitable, or where people can't work outdoors in the summer. If we don't solve the biodiversity crisis, the prospects are even worse.” Gorte said. “So there are things that we have to do in order to preserve what we think of as life as we know it, and those drivers are going to remain in place.”

#7627. Ex-Denver Nuggets player, attorney settle malpractice lawsuit

NBA player Chris “Birdman” Andersen, then of the Miami Heat, looks on before taking on the San Antonio Spurs on June 6, 2013, in Miami. (Photo by Mike Ehrmann/Getty Images)

Former NBA player Chris “Birdman” Andersen has settled a legal malpractice lawsuit with his attorney, whom Andersen claimed failed to protect his intellectual property and ruined his in-laws’ creperie business.

According to a joint notice of settlement filed Tuesday in Colorado state court, Andersen and lawyer Mark L. Byant reached a settlement during mediation Monday and asked the court to vacate deadlines in the case which had a trial scheduled for Dec. 7. Terms were not disclosed.

The former player for the Denver Nuggets sued Bryant in 2024 for allegedly misappropriating his funds; allegedly failing to resolve his liability; and allegedly providing family members with negligent advice, along with the intellectual property claims.

Andersen claims that in 2022, former NBA star Shaquille O’Neal’s production company Jersey Legends in collaboration with another production company wanted to produce a documentary about Andersen’s life and career, including his victimization in a catfishing scheme. But without Andersen’s knowledge, Bryant signed a collaboration agreement almost identical to a draft that Andersen found unacceptable, according to the complaint, “forever” restricting Andersen’s ability to participate in other projects related to his life story and the scheme.

Andersen said he has “received zero compensation as a result of the project” that Netflix agreed to distribute.
